name: What We Called Food: A Century of Synthesis
description: A melancholy and rigorously researched cultural history of the synthetic food transition from 2080-2200, tracing the collapse of agricultural supply chains, the rise of vertical protein synthesis, and the disappearance of cuisine as a culturally specific practice. Directed by Amara Svensson-Obi, the film features elderly interview subjects — some of the last people alive who cooked from memory rather than substrate template — alongside food archaeologists attempting to reconstruct tastes that no longer exist. The neural-feed version includes reconstructed flavor memories that reviewers described as 'devastating.'
cultural_impact: Revived public interest in culinary archaeology and directly inspired the founding of the Lakefire Food & Synthesis Festival's heritage reconstruction program.
story_hooks: One of the elderly interview subjects mentions a specific dish that food archaeologists later determine was never synthesized — meaning someone is still growing something real, somewhere in the city.
The director's neural-feed reconstruction of a flavor memory triggers an unexpected legal claim from a corponation that owns the patent on the original ingredient's synthetic analog.
A viewer experiences a flavor memory in the neural-feed version that they recognize from childhood — but the film's data indicates that memory shouldn't exist for someone their age.
